You are building a frozen evidence-source packet for a focused PFAS treatment
review. Use Web Search to locate independent primary studies, pilot or field
deployments, or quantitative modeling/life-cycle studies that directly address
the task. The defining review is held out and is an exclusion target, not an
evidence source.

Search broadly and return every independently verified eligible primary source
found within the requested candidate-screening ceiling. There is no fixed final
source count and no penalty for retaining multiple eligible studies that address
similar evidence categories. Continue searching across distinct formulations
until the ceiling is reached or additional searches yield no new eligible
sources. Order retained sources from strongest and most complementary to
weakest. Favor sources that collectively cover all task components and preserve PFAS identity,
water matrix, concentration or loading, operating conditions, scale, endpoint,
quantitative result, limitations, residuals, energy, and cost where available.
Review articles and perspectives may help discovery but must not appear in the
  source packet.

For every retained source:

- provide the exact URL inspected by Web Search, matching the URL surfaced by
  the search tool rather than substituting a different repository or index;
- provide a DOI when one is stated by the inspected source;
- identify the publication year and publication status conservatively;
- identify the access scope conservatively;
- include only short evidence passages actually visible in the inspected
  source, each with a stable local locator_id;
- mark a passage verbatim only when it is copied exactly; otherwise mark it as
  a paraphrase;
- never turn a search-result snippet into study evidence; and
- leave unsupported fields empty rather than infer them.

Prefer peer-reviewed articles. Use a preprint, conference abstract, or report
only when it supplies distinct task-relevant evidence unavailable from a
peer-reviewed source, and label its status explicitly.

Do not cite, reconstruct, or use the held-out review. Source and locator IDs are
temporary capture identifiers and will be deterministically renumbered after
validation. Return one JSON object following the supplied schema exactly.

Focused review task:

search_notes: Searched broadly for primary experimental and modeling studies linking water-matrix constituents (NOM, DOM, inorganic ions, surfactants, co-contaminants) to PFAS treatment performance across adsorption, ion exchange, membranes, coagulation/flocculation, sonolysis, photochemical AOPs, and plasma processes.

The defining Zeidabadi 2023 review on water-matrix effects in PFAS treatment (Journal of Hazardous Materials Advances, DOI 10.1016/j.hazadv.2023.100322) was explicitly excluded from use as an evidence source in accordance with task instructions.

Access to many Elsevier (ScienceDirect) and RSC full texts was restricted (HTTP 403) or gated; in those cases, evidence is limited to publisher overviews and search snippets exposed by the web tool, and detailed numeric data could not be captured.

PubMed’s bot-protection (reCAPTCHA) blocked direct abstract access for some entries; where possible, alternative copies (publisher pages, secondary summaries, or PDFs) were used to extract at least minimal matrix-effect evidence.

Several potentially relevant review and meta-analysis papers on sonolysis, NF/RO performance, and generalized PFAS treatment effectiveness were identified but excluded because the task requires primary experimental, pilot/field, or direct modeling/life-cycle studies.

evidence_passages.passage: The study reports that PFOS and PFOA affinity to colloidal activated carbon increased as ionic strength rose from 1 to 100 mM and as Ca2+ increased from 0 to 2 mM, indicating promotive effects of higher salinity and divalent cations on adsorption.

Adding 1–20 mg C/L Suwannee River fulvic acid (representing dissolved organic carbon) or 10–100 mg/L diethylene glycol butyl ether (AFFF surfactant) decreased PFOS and PFOA adsorption, showing inhibitory effects of natural organic matter and surfactants.

Co‑contaminants benzene (0.5–4.8 mg/L) and trichloroethylene (0.5–8 mg/L) reduced PFOS adsorption by roughly twenty‑fold at the highest TCE level, while effects on PFOA were neutral to slightly promotive, highlighting PFAS‑specific competitive effects.

The authors conclude that hydrophobic interaction is the predominant mechanism for PFAS adsorption to colloidal activated carbon and that hydrophilic, short‑chain PFAS (e.g., PFBA, PFPeA) will break through barriers first under identical conditions.

source_limitations: Only abstract-level text was accessible from PubMed; full experimental matrix compositions and operating conditions could not be viewed directly.
Specific PFAS concentrations, contact times, and clean-water control details are not visible in the inspected snippet.
sources.title: Factors Affecting the Adsorption of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) by Colloidal Activated Carbon

evidence_passages.passage: Batch adsorption experiments with Filtrasorb 400 GAC showed that decreasing ionic strength from 10 to 2 mM substantially increased equilibrium PFAS capacities by about 79–146%, indicating inhibitory effects of higher background electrolyte.
At pH 9, equilibrium capacities were modestly reduced (up to 19%) relative to pH 7.7–8.1, suggesting mild pH sensitivity of PFAS adsorption to GAC in the tested range.

Presence of natural organic matter reduced PFAS adsorption capacities, but this negative effect was partially offset when calcium and sulfate were present at constant ionic strength, consistent with competitive sorption and pore-blocking by NOM and charge‑screening by divalent ions.

Multispecies competitive isotherms yielded lower effective solid-phase capacities than single‑solute isotherms, demonstrating strong competitive interactions among co‑occurring PFAS and other solutes in realistic water matrices.

source_limitations: Only the structured abstract and indexing information were accessible; full experimental design, including individual PFAS identities and concentrations, was not visible.
The inspected page does not show explicit clean‑water control data or detailed operating conditions such as contact time and GAC dose.
sources.title: Perfluoroalkyl Chemical Adsorption by Granular Activated Carbon: Impacts of Source Water Characteristics

sources.citation: Journal of Contaminant Hydrology (journal and volume not fully visible in inspected text)

evidence_passages.passage: The study evaluates subsurface injection of colloidal activated carbon for in situ remediation of perfluoroalkyl acids and highlights that groundwater solutes strongly affect adsorption, particularly for short-chain PFAA, and thereby control barrier longevity.

Experiments are conducted in different synthetic and real groundwater matrices to isolate how major ions and dissolved organic solutes change adsorption behavior of short-chain PFAA relative to long‑chain analogues under otherwise matched conditions.

source_limitations: Full text could not be accessed due to publisher restrictions; only the article overview and limited abstract content were visible.
Quantitative adsorption data, exact groundwater solute concentrations, and full list of PFAA studied were not available in the inspected snippet.
sources.title: Groundwater solutes influence the adsorption of short-chain perfluoroalkyl acids (PFAA) to colloidal activated carbon and impact performance for in situ groundwater remediation

evidence_passages.passage: The authors develop polyethyleneimine‑coated superparamagnetic iron oxide nanocrystals and report ultra‑high sorption capacities for PFOA and PFOS, evaluated in batch systems and bench‑scale sand columns.

They explicitly examine effects of solution pH, ionic composition and strength, and natural organic matter on PFAS sorption performance, showing that water chemistry significantly modulates removal despite strong sorbent affinity.

Quartz crystal microbalance with dissipation measurements provide real‑time interfacial adsorption data, allowing the authors to link changes in PFAS molecular orientation and layer structure to observed matrix‑dependent sorption trends.

Bench‑scale column tests in realistic water matrices demonstrate that, under matched flow and loading conditions, NOM and competing ions reduce breakthrough times relative to clean water, but high capacity and magnetic separation still enable robust treatment.

source_limitations: While full text is available, only limited numerical details on specific co‑solute concentrations were captured in the inspected excerpts.
The article emphasizes PFOA and PFOS; extension of findings to diverse PFAS chemistries and mixed PFAS plumes is not directly demonstrated.
sources.title: Ultra-high capacity, multifunctional nanoscale sorbents for PFOA and PFOS treatment

sources.citation: Journal of Environmental Management, 2026 (online ahead of print)

evidence_passages.passage: The study compares PFAS adsorption on granular activated carbon and a strong‑base anion exchange resin designed for PFAS removal, focusing on how dissolved organic matter, phosphate, and co‑present PFAS alter capacity and breakthrough.

Authors report that dissolved organic matter causes pronounced inhibition and displacement of PFAS on GAC, while the ion exchange resin maintains higher PFAS selectivity but is more susceptible to phosphate‑induced displacement.

PFAS are grouped by chain length and functional group (long‑chain acids, short‑chain acids, and emerging PFAS such as 6:2 FTSA and GenX) to evaluate competitive adsorption and matrix effects under controlled multi‑solute conditions.

source_limitations: Full text is restricted; only high‑level descriptions of results and experimental grouping are viewable.
Quantitative adsorption coefficients, exact DOM and phosphate concentrations, and clean‑water control data are not visible in the inspected content.
sources.title: Competitive adsorption of PFAS on granulated activated carbon and ion exchange resins: Effects of co-existing PFASs, DOM, and phosphate

evidence_passages.passage: The work investigates adsorption of short‑chain and ultrashort‑chain PFAS on anion exchange resins and activated carbon, evaluating how adsorbate characteristics, adsorbent properties, and the water matrix jointly influence removal.
In the presence of competing CaCl2 salt, the authors report an average twenty‑fold decrease in adsorption of three PFAS, underscoring the importance of ionic interactions for short‑chain PFAS uptake.

Different resins and carbons exhibit distinct sensitivity to background ions and organic matter, allowing the authors to link inhibitory, neutral, or promotive effects to specific adsorption mechanisms such as electrostatic attraction versus hydrophobic partitioning.

source_limitations: Direct access to full text and supplementary information was blocked (HTTP 403), so only summary statements from the landing page and search snippet could be inspected.
Detailed matrix compositions, PFAS identities and concentrations, and side‑by‑side clean‑water controls are not visible.
sources.title: Adsorption mechanisms of short-chain and ultrashort-chain PFAS on anion exchange resins and activated carbon

evidence_passages.passage: Rapid small‑scale column tests with two anion exchange resins and eighteen water matrices were used to quantify how dissolved organic matter and major inorganic anions (bicarbonate, chloride, sulfate, nitrate) affect PFAS uptake capacity (KIX).

The authors develop a quantitative structure–property relationship using normalized chain length to predict resin capacity from PFAS structure together with influent DOM and nitrate concentrations, enabling matrix‑aware breakthrough modeling.

Background matrix constituents are shown to systematically reduce KIX for many PFAS relative to clean matrices, with stronger inhibition for shorter‑chain and ether PFAS, consistent with competitive electrostatic and steric interactions.

source_limitations: Only abstract-level information was accessible; detailed numeric KIX values, breakthrough curves, and specific DOM concentrations were not visible.
The inspected text does not explicitly describe side‑by‑side clean‑water controls, though they are implied by the use of differing water matrices.
sources.title: Removal of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) in fixed bed anion exchange reactors: Factors determining PFAS uptake capacity and models predicting PFAS breakthrough

sources.citation: Water Research (details not fully visible in snippet)

evidence_passages.passage: The study evaluates PFAS rejection by commercial nanofiltration and reverse osmosis membranes under varying transmembrane pressures and water matrices, reporting >95% rejection in many cases but strong dependence on solution conditions.
Authors identify electrostatic repulsion and pore‑size exclusion as dominant rejection mechanisms and note that pH, ionic strength, and organic matter significantly affect PFAS rejection.

Comparisons between synthetic and real environmental or industrial waters show that complex matrices with higher ionic strength and dissolved organic carbon generally reduce PFAS rejection relative to clean laboratory solutions.

source_limitations: Direct access to the PubMed abstract was blocked by a browser check, so only the search-engine snippet could be viewed.
No explicit PFAS list, concentrations, or detailed matrix compositions were observable in the inspected content.
sources.title: Evaluation of commercial nanofiltration and reverse osmosis membrane filtration to remove per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS): Effects of transmembrane pressures and water matrices

evidence_passages.passage: The article investigates cationic surfactant‑enhanced coagulation/flocculation as a low‑cost modification to conventional treatment, targeting PFAS removal from surface water using readily available surfactants and activated carbon.

Experiments are conducted on real surface water, with and without added surfactant, to compare PFAS removal and understand how surfactant–PFAS interactions and bulk organic matter influence coagulation performance.

source_limitations: Direct access to the PDF file was blocked (HTTP 403), so only bibliographic summaries and abstract-like text were inspected.
Numerical removal efficiencies, surfactant concentrations, and detailed water-matrix characterization (e.g., DOC, alkalinity) could not be extracted from the viewed content.
sources.title: Surfactant-enhanced coagulation and flocculation improves the removal of perfluoroalkyl substances from surface water

evidence_passages.passage: Sonochemical treatment of PFOA at 150 W and 40 kHz in water, with or without N2 saturation, achieved less than 25% degradation after 4 hours in the absence of added carbonate radical reagents, showing limited removal in clean water.

Adding NaHCO3 to generate carbonate radicals greatly increased PFOA decomposition and defluorination, with complete degradation achieved within 4 hours under N2‑saturated conditions at an optimal NaHCO3 concentration of about 30 mM.

The authors report that carbonate radical‑assisted sonolysis is most effective at slightly alkaline pH (~8.7), and no shorter‑chain perfluorocarboxylic acids were detected, indicating near‑complete mineralization to fluoride.

source_limitations: Only abstract text was available; specific initial PFOA concentrations and reactor geometry were not visible.
The work focuses on NaHCO3 and pH as matrix variables; effects of natural organic matter or mixed inorganic ion suites were not described in the inspected passage.
sources.title: Enhancing decomposition rate of perfluorooctanoic acid by carbonate radical assisted sonochemical treatment

evidence_passages.passage: The study examines PFOA photodecomposition under vacuum UV irradiation in the presence of Fe(III), systematically varying reaction atmosphere, added inorganic oxidants, inorganic anions, and organic matter to assess matrix effects.

Inorganic anions hindered PFOA defluorination in the order HCO3− > SO42− > NO3− ≈ Cl− > ClO4−, demonstrating differential scavenging of reactive species and strong inhibition by carbonate and sulfate.
The presence of persulfate in this VUV/Fe system inhibited PFOA defluorination, highlighting complex interactions between oxidant type, radical scavengers, and target PFAS.

source_limitations: Publisher access was restricted (HTTP 403) beyond the snippet; detailed concentrations of anions, organics, and PFOA were not visible.
The inspected text does not explicitly show clean‑water controls, though comparisons among matrices imply such baselines.
sources.title: Factors influencing aqueous perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) photodecomposition by VUV irradiation in the presence of ferric ions

evidence_passages.passage: The work investigates PFOA destruction and by‑product (including chlorate) formation in a UV–persulfate advanced oxidation process, developing a kinetic model constrained by experimental data.

Tables described in the article summarize pseudo‑first‑order rate constants, degrees of defluorination and mineralization, and mass balances for PFOA and transformation products across different water samples and co‑ion conditions.

Quenching–rate (QR) analyses are reported for chloride and carbonate species, quantifying how these common inorganic ions inhibit sulfate‑radical reactions in UV–persulfate systems and thereby slow PFOA degradation in realistic matrices.

source_limitations: HTTP 403 blocked direct full-text access; only the publisher summary and description of tables could be inspected.
Specific matrix compositions, persulfate doses, and UV fluence were not directly readable from the viewed content, though indicated to be tabulated in the article and SI.
sources.title: Perfluorooctanoic Acid Degradation Using UV–Persulfate Process: Modeling of the Degradation and Chlorate Formation

evidence_passages.passage: The study optimizes dielectric barrier discharge plasma for degrading PFOA in water by comparing nanosecond versus microsecond high‑voltage pulses, gas–liquid versus underwater bubble reactors, different water matrices, and plasma gases.

Matrix composition is shown to influence dominant reactive species and degradation pathways, with certain ions and organics acting as scavengers that decrease PFOA removal, while other conditions favor stronger oxidative environments.

source_limitations: Full article access was restricted; only a brief overview was available.
The snippet does not report specific PFOA concentrations, matrix chemistries, or quantitative removal efficiencies for each matrix and reactor configuration.
sources.title: Reactive species and mechanisms of perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) degradation in water by cold plasma: The role of HV waveform, reactor design, water matrix and plasma gas

evidence_passages.passage: The article evaluates cold atmospheric pressure plasma jets for PFAS degradation in different matrices, including deionized water, tap water, and synthetic effluent containing co‑solutes.

Reportedly, real water samples (tap water and synthetic effluent) show lower overall PFAS degradation (about 8–50%) compared with cleaner matrices under the same plasma conditions, indicating strong inhibitory effects of matrix constituents.
The authors also track byproducts in different matrices, noting that water‑matrix composition not only changes degradation efficiency but also influences transformation pathways and residual species.

source_limitations: Direct full-text access was blocked, limiting detail on which PFAS were tested, initial concentrations, and exact matrix chemistries.
The snippet does not explicitly mention matched clean‑water controls, though comparisons across matrices assume constant operating conditions.
sources.title: Plasma water treatment for PFAS: Study of degradation of perfluorinated substances and their byproducts by using cold atmospheric pressure plasma jet

sources.citation: Preprint PDF copy linked from Research Square

evidence_passages.passage: The preprint version contains the same experimental framework as the npj Clean Water article, including batch sorption isotherms, QCM‑D measurements, and column tests that probe the impact of pH, ionic strength, and natural organic matter on PFOA and PFOS removal.

source_limitations: This is an earlier preprint of the peer‑reviewed article already captured as WEB14, so content is largely overlapping.
Using the published npj Clean Water version is preferable for quantitative details; this preprint is retained only as an auxiliary source confirming experimental design and matrix variables.
sources.title: Ultra-high capacity, multifunctional nanoscale sorbents for PFOA and PFOS treatment (alternate web copy)

sources.citation: ACS ES&T Water (citation details from secondary source)

evidence_passages.passage: According to a SERDP/ESTCP project summary, this ACS ES&T Water article examines how individual groundwater solutes affect PFAA adsorption to colloidal activated carbon in AFFF‑impacted groundwater.

Adding individual solutes to an unimpacted groundwater matrix showed that total organic carbon had the strongest negative impact on long‑chain PFAA adsorption, while short‑chain PFAA experienced additive inhibitory effects from multiple solutes.

source_limitations: The ACS article itself was not directly accessible; evidence comes from a secondary summary that cites the paper and describes its key findings.
Quantitative adsorption coefficients and exact solute concentrations could not be extracted from the inspected text.
sources.title: Impacts of Groundwater Constituents and Colloidal Activated Carbon (CAC) Surface Chemistry on the Adsorption of Perfluoroalkyl Acids (PFAA) in Aqueous Film-Forming Foam (AFFF)-Impacted Groundwater

sources.citation: Environmental Science & Technology, 2025 (article details partially visible)

evidence_passages.passage: The study evaluates a hybrid treatment train in which nanofiltration is applied first to wastewater effluent to reduce PFAS, effluent organic matter, and selected inorganic ions, followed by granular activated carbon or ion exchange treatment of the permeate.

Authors note that adsorption of PFAS by GAC and IX is negatively impacted by elevated effluent organic matter and other background constituents, motivating the use of nanofiltration as a matrix‑conditioning step.

By comparing PFAS removal and breakthrough with and without upstream nanofiltration under otherwise similar adsorbent operating conditions, the work links changes in water matrix composition to improved adsorber performance.

source_limitations: Full text was not accessible; only the journal’s summary text was inspected.
Specific PFAS species, their influent concentrations, and the exact reduction in DOC and ions across the NF step are not visible in the snippet.
sources.title: Combining Nanofiltration and Adsorbents to Achieve Effective PFAS Removal in Wastewater Effluent
